Transcript:
[00:00:04] Amy (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Priya, Marcus, Jordan, Leah — great to see you. We're going to demo a concrete inventory use case today: structured actions for "restock recommendation" plus a console tour of JSON mode and safety guardrails. Mateo will lead the technical bits.

[00:00:22] Priya (Cascadia): Thanks Amy. Quick context: our goal is to automate low-stock alerts and trigger restock actions into our procurement pipeline. The big asks are strong typed outputs, auditable logs, and the ability to run in our VPC or a dedicated tenancy because of supplier contracts. Also cost matters.

[00:00:40] Mateo (Redwood SE): Great. We'll show you how Redwood's JSON-mode enforces a schema for actions — so the model returns a typed payload like {"action": "restock", "sku": "ABC123", "qty": 100, "priority": "high"} — and how the runtime validates and only allows sanctioned fields. Note: transcription may call KV cash instead of KV cache sometimes in the notes.

[00:01:03] Jordan (Cascadia): Two quick infra constraints: we want all PII and supplier pricing to stay in our VPC; KMS-managed keys are mandatory. Also curious about latency — our alert pipeline needs sub-300ms median generation for single-SKU checks.

[00:01:20] Amy (Redwood AE): Yep, we can cover latency profiles. For single-item lookups most teams see sub-200ms on Dedicated in-region; Hosted can be tuned too. We'll show batching options as well because when you run bulk checks throughput matters.

[00:02:05] Mateo (Redwood SE): Jumping into the Console — I'm sharing my screen now — bear with me, I have a sample schema open. The schema defines an "Action" object with enum actionType [restock, hold, escalate], sku string, qty integer, confidence float, and optional supplierId. The JSON-mode runtime will reject extra fields and return a structured error if the model adds unexpected keys.

[00:03:10] [00:03:12] Mateo (Redwood SE): Example prompt + schema enforcement: we seed the prompt with last-known stock, lead times, and sales velocity. Console shows a live preview of the typed response and a validation trace. Sometimes the trace says "alpha fallback" when a smaller model is used — that's our automatic fallback to cheaper variants if the primary is overloaded.

[00:04:01] Leah (Cascadia): If the model falls back to a smaller variant, how does the runtime preserve correctness? We can't have bad restock quantities.

[00:04:14] Mateo (Redwood SE): Good question. We have quality thresholds tied to model profiles. If the fallback's expected accuracy drops below a configured threshold for that prompt-set, the runtime can either block the action and call a human-in-loop or attach a higher audit score and route to a verification queue. You can configure per-route rules in the Console.

[00:05:05] Priya (Cascadia): Walk me through audit logs — we need immutable records of every action with the model version, input hashing, and KMS-wrapped keys.

[00:05:16] Amy (Redwood AE): We capture token-level traces, model hash/version, and a signed proof of the schema validation outcome. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and retain logs in your S3 or on-prem store — audit trail meets SOC2-like needs. There may be small transcription artifacts in the notes where we say "signed proof" as "sine proof" sometimes.

[00:06:02] Jordan (Cascadia): On the network side, VPC peering and private IPs are critical. How does Redwood Private handle peering?

[00:06:12] Mateo (Redwood SE): Private provides a customer-controlled control plane and can deploy inference nodes inside a customer VPC or in a peered subnet. We can also do an on-prem package for fully air-gapped needs. We'll share our network diagram and the peering playbook after this call.

[00:07:05] [00:07:07] Mateo (Redwood SE): Back to JSON-mode: here's an example where the model attempted to include a human note field. Console's schema guard stripped it and recorded a validation error: "unexpected_field: human_note". The request still returned a rejection payload with an explanation, so your downstream webhook won't receive malformed JSON.

[00:08:30] Marcus (Cascadia): For action invocation, can Redwood directly call our procurement API, or do we need a middleware? We prefer an event-driven webhook triggered by validated actions.

[00:08:45] Amy (Redwood AE): You can do either. The runtime supports function/tool calling where the validated payload is emitted as a typed event. We have built-in webhooks and also integrations with orchestration tools. The Console shows a mapping where you can map action fields to endpoint parameters and set retry/backoff policies.

[00:09:28] Priya (Cascadia): How do you prevent hallucinated SKUs or supplier IDs — we can't allow bad supplier assignments.

[00:09:40] Mateo (Redwood SE): We do whitelist verification at runtime: you can provide a canonical catalog (as a lookup table or prefix cache). The model's output sku is checked against the catalog. If not found, it's either rejected or flagged for review depending on policy. We also surface a confidence field and provenance tokens so you can trace what evidence the model used.

[00:10:22] [00:10:25] Mateo (Redwood SE): Quick demo of the Optimize tab: it shows batching stats, token costs, and suggestions like turning on KV cache for static SKU metadata, or enabling int8 quantization on dedicated pools to reduce token cost by ~30% on certain models.

[00:11:05] Jordan (Cascadia): That quantization — does it affect numeric accuracy in the qty field? We need exact integers for order quantities.

[00:11:16] Mateo (Redwood SE): Quantization impacts float computations in models; but since qty is a generated integer, we recommend using post-validate rounding plus schema enforcement. The runtime will coerce to the schema type and if coercion fails, it rejects the response. For mission-critical flows we suggest Dedicated with tested quant profiles, or run a quick eval on your SKU prompts.

[00:12:00] [00:12:04] Amy (Redwood AE): Another feature: rollout policies. You can canary the JSON-mode contract on, say, 10% of traffic and compare action correctness and latency. Console will surface regressions and let you rollback. Useful when you change prompt templates or upgrade model variants.

[00:12:50] Priya (Cascadia): Can we run a POC with a single warehouse region first? Want to see end-to-end with real telemetry.

[00:13:02] Amy (Redwood AE): Absolutely. Typical POC: 4 weeks, start with 3-5 SKUs, integrate webhooks, run comparison against current rules engine. We'll provide a template pilot contract.

[00:13:30] Marcus (Cascadia): Pricing — we need Hosted numbers and Dedicated commit pricing. Also what's the uplift for Private + KMS-managed keys?

[00:13:45] Amy (Redwood AE): I'll send a TCO sheet with hosted per-token pricing, and a Dedicated example with reserved GPU pool pricing, including optional private control plane costs. KMS integrations are an add-on for Private; I'll include rough estimates.

[00:14:20] [00:14:22] Leah (Cascadia): A security question: how do you handle secrets in prompts? Our product keys are sensitive.

[00:14:34] Mateo (Redwood SE): Don't put secrets in prompts. Instead use secure references: the runtime can fetch secrets at call time using your KMS/HSM and inject ephemeral tokens into the model environment, or better, perform lookups server-side and pass non-sensitive contextual signals into the prompt. We'll share a best-practices doc.

[00:15:10] Priya (Cascadia): Any known limitations for catalog sizes? We have a catalog of 1.2M SKUs.

[00:15:20] Mateo (Redwood SE): For very large catalogs we recommend a hybrid approach: prefix filtering in your DB and then small candidate lists into the prompt + prefix caching on the runtime. Our KV cache is optimized for common SKU sets and can be warmed during startup. We'll include an architecture note for large catalog handling.

[00:16:05] [00:16:08] Mateo (Redwood SE): Demo: I trigger a sample request with three SKUs — Console shows the typed responses, validation traces, and the webhook payload ready to send. You can toggle a simulated fallback and see that the runtime either annotates the payload with a "fallback" flag or blocks it per policy.

[00:17:30] Jordan (Cascadia): Can the console export the validation traces for our compliance team? They need a CSV with model version, input hash, output hash, and validation result.

[00:17:42] Amy (Redwood AE): Yes, exports are supported; you can also ship logs to your S3 bucket with encryption using your KMS.

[00:18:20] Priya (Cascadia): Any reference customers in retail who did a similar flow?

[00:18:32] Amy (Redwood AE): We have a mid-market retail customer (anonymized) that used JSON-mode for order routing and saw 40% fewer false positives vs their rules engine after tuning. I can share a redacted case study.

[00:19:05] [00:19:08] Mateo (Redwood SE): Quick note on function/tool calling: Console supports idempotency keys for action invocations and built-in retry logic. If you map an action to a procurement endpoint we can automatically ensure at-most-once semantics if the backend supports it.

[00:20:00] Marcus (Cascadia): What about regulatory compliance — data residency? We have EU contracts and need logs to stay in eu-central region for some suppliers.

[00:20:12] Amy (Redwood AE): We can pin deployments by region for Dedicated and Private. Hosted offers regional endpoints as well; for strict residency we recommend Private in-region or a Dedicated reserved pool in eu-central.

[00:21:05] [00:21:08] Priya (Cascadia): For the pilot success criteria, we'll measure: accuracy vs current rules (target +10% precision), latency under 300ms median, and end-to-end failed action rate below 1%.

[00:21:30] Amy (Redwood AE): Sounds good. We'll target those metrics in the pilot proposal.

[00:22:00] Mateo (Redwood SE): Demo wrap-up: I'll upload the schema file and the Console recording. The schema sample includes validation policy snippets and a sample webhook mapping.

[00:22:35] [00:22:37] Leah (Cascadia): If we need to escalate to a security review, who do we loop in?

[00:22:44] Amy (Redwood AE): I'll bring in our security & compliance lead, Sanjay, and we can do a SOC2/ISO security deep-dive. We typically run an architecture review call.

[00:23:15] Priya (Cascadia): Timeline question — if we sign a pilot by end of month, how quickly can we be live?

[00:23:26] Amy (Redwood AE): For a scoped pilot with 3 SKUs we can typically stand up in 2–3 weeks, assuming we get telemetry access and network peering details.

[00:24:10] Jordan (Cascadia): Are there any hard limits on concurrency per route on Dedicated? We plan to run several hundred checks per second during peak.

[00:24:22] Mateo (Redwood SE): Dedicated allows you to size GPU pools; we can guarantee throughput with autoscaling policies. We'll size an example pool for your expected RPS and share latency percentiles under load.

[00:25:00] [00:25:03] Marcus (Cascadia): One more question on fallback: do you keep a separate log of which requests hit fallback models so we can audit them later?

[00:25:14] Mateo (Redwood SE): Yes, fallback events are logged with model variant, reason for fallback (e.g., capacity, cost-policy), and the original request trace. You can query those in Console or export them.

[00:25:50] Amy (Redwood AE): Ok quick recap and actions: Amy will send pricing and TCO; Mateo will share the console recording, schema examples, and peering playbook; Priya & Jordan will send sample telemetry and confirm pilot SKUs. Any other open items?

[00:26:08] Priya (Cascadia): Could you include a sample SLO doc and rollback playbook for the pilot — we want clear error budgets.

[00:26:18] Amy (Redwood AE): Yes, we'll include a sample SLO and can walk through the rollback plan in the next call.

[00:27:00] [00:27:03] Mateo (Redwood SE): Small demo glitch — the Console simulated a validation false-positive; note that sometimes the auto-transcription here will say "false positive" as "vault positive". This is just a transcript artifact.

[00:28:20] Priya (Cascadia): Ok let's talk about legal and vendors — any standard contractual terms around data retention and deletion?

[00:28:32] Amy (Redwood AE): We have standard DPA terms and retention configs; for Private we can align retention to your policy and add an NDA/data handling appendix as needed. Legal can follow up after the pilot scope is confirmed.

[00:29:10] Marcus (Cascadia): Are there recommended evals to run before we go to 100%? Like a precision/recall sweep?

[00:29:22] Mateo (Redwood SE): Yes, we recommend a labeled test-set (50–200 examples) per SKU class to measure precision/recall and then a smaller live shadow test. We'll help you design the eval harness.

[00:30:05] Amy (Redwood AE): Final quick note: I'll include competitor differentiation — some customers move from our competitors because of better runtime guardrails and tighter observability for structured outputs. Will share a short competitor matrix.

[00:30:30] [00:30:35] Priya (Cascadia): Great. Let's confirm next meeting — a pilot kickoff demo with infra folks next Wednesday?

[00:30:44] Amy (Redwood AE): How about Oct 21st at 10am PT?

[00:31:05] Jordan (Cascadia): Works.

[00:31:15] Marcus (Cascadia): Works.

[00:31:35] [00:31:38] Mateo (Redwood SE): Ok that's the end of the demo portion. If you want I'll leave the rest of the Console open to poke around.

[00:31:50] Priya (Cascadia): Thanks Mateo — that helped a lot. One last small ask: can you show the exact webhook example payload that arrives after schema validation?

[00:32:02] Mateo (Redwood SE): Sure, it's in the recording and I'll paste the snippet in the follow-up note. It looks like: {"action":"restock","sku":"AB-12345","qty":50,"confidence":0.92,"validation":"ok","model_version":"rwd-v2.1"}.

[00:32:40] Leah (Cascadia): Good, that matches what we expected.

[00:33:00] Amy (Redwood AE): Great. We'll send the follow-up including: TCO, schema samples, console recording, peering playbook, SLO template, and pilot statement of work.
